body: ABDUL FAYAZ, J.- Through the instant appeal under Section 17(2) of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Consumers Protection Act, 1997, United Bank Limited has called in question the judgment dated 13.04.2026 passed by the learned Consumer Court, Abbottabad, whereby the complaint filed by respondent Mst. Nasreen Akhtar was allowed.

2. Briefly stated, the respondent maintained a Profit and Loss Sharing (PLS) account with the appellant Bank at its Pine View Branch, Abbottabad. Her case before the learned Consumer Court was that the Bank had converted her PLS account into a current account without obtaining her consent. She approached the Bank for restoration of the original status of the account. Her grievance remained unresolved, whereupon she filed a complaint before the learned Consumer Court, Abbottabad. The learned Consumer Court summoned the parties and, after hearing them, allowed the complaint. Aggrieved, the Bank has preferred this appeal.
3. Arguments heard and available record gone through.

4. The question for determination is “whether the learned Consumer Court had jurisdiction to entertain a complaint seeking reversal of the Bank’s decision to convert the respondent’s PLS account into a current account?”
5. Section 2 (c) of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Consumer Protection Act, 1997 defines Consumer as;

“Consumer means any person or entity who;- (i) Buys goods for a consideration which has been paid or to promised or partly paid and partly promised to be paid or under any system of deferred payment including hire purchase and leasing and includes any use of such goods but does not include a person who obtains such goods for re-sale or for any commercial purpose; or (ii) Hires any goods or services for a consideration which has been paid or promised or partly paid and partly promises to be paid or under any system of deferred payment including hire purchase and leasing and includes any beneficiary of such services.”
Section 2(n) of the Act of 1997 defines “services” as;

“Services includes services of any description which are made available to potential users and includes the provisions of facilities in connection with banking, financing, insurance, transport, manufacturing, processing, accountancy, supply of electrical, mechanical or any other form of energy including gas and petrol, water, telephone, boarding or lodging, entertainment, medicine, education, construction work, amusement, catering, security, or purveying news or other information and similar other services but does not include the rendering of any service free of charge or under the contract or personal services”

While sub-section (4) of Section (1) of the Act of 1997, provides a saving clause which is also reproduced hereinbelow for ready reference; “Save as otherwise expressly exempted by Government through a notification in the official gazette, this Act shall apply to all goods and services.”
Meaning thereby that the Act of 1997 shall apply to all goods and services, except those expressly exempted by the Government through a notification in official Gazette.

6. This Court in order to answer the question relating to the jurisdiction of the learned Consumer Court in the case in hand, has to determine as to whether the services provided by the appellant were expressly exempted by the Government or not. Section 18 of the Federal Ombudsmen Institutional Reforms Act, 2013 bars a court or authority from entertaining a matter falling within the jurisdiction of an Ombudsman. It also bars a court or authority from assuming jurisdiction over a matter pending with or decided by an Ombudsman. The first limb turns on the nature of the matter and applies even where no complaint has yet been lodged before the Ombudsman. The Act of 2013 applies to the statutory scheme governing the Banking Mohtasib, and Section 24 gives its provisions overriding effect. When Section 1(4) and Section 3 of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Consumer Protection Act, 1997 are read in juxtaposition with Section 18 and 24 of the Federal Ombudsmen Institutional Reforms Act, 2013, the jurisdiction of learned Consumer Court stands excluded in the services provided by the Banks as the matter falls within the jurisdiction of Banking Mohtasib.

7. Section 12 of the Consumer Protection Act, 1997, regulates the territorial jurisdiction of the Consumer Court, while Section 13(1)(a) enables a consumer to lodge a complaint in relation to a service provided to him or her. Section 3 provides that the Act operates in addition to other laws and preserves their operation. Accordingly, even where the relationship of consumer and service provider exists and the complaint concerns a service within the meaning of the Act, the Consumer Court must give effect to an applicable statutory bar governing the particular subject matter of the complaint.

8. Section 82-A(3)(a) of the Banking Companies Ordinance, 1962 empowers the Banking Mohtasib to inquire into complaints of banking malpractices. Section 82-A(3)(c) extends that jurisdiction to alleged violations of banking laws, rules, regulations or guidelines. Section 82-B(4)(a) empowers the Mohtasib to entertain complaints from bank customers, among others. Section 82-B(5)(a)(i) applies to all banks operating in Pakistan and covers complaints alleging failure to comply with banking laws and regulations, including policy directives or guidelines issued by the State Bank of Pakistan. Its proviso requires a dispute concerning the proper interpretation of such regulations, directions or guidelines to be referred to the State Bank for clarification.

9. Section 82-B(5)(b) confers additional jurisdiction in respect of public-sector banks on grounds of corrupt or mala fide practices by bank officers, gross dereliction of duty in dealing with customers, and inordinate delays in taking decisions. The appellant Bank was privatized in 2002. Its amenability to the jurisdiction of the Banking Mohtasib in the present matter accordingly falls to be examined under Section 82-A(3), read with Sections 82-B(4)(a) and 82-B(5)(a)(i). The remedies available under Section 82-E(1) include directing the Bank to reconsider, modify or cancel the impugned action. The relief sought by the respondent, i.e. the restoration of the original status of her account, is of the kind that the Banking Mohtasib is empowered to consider.

10. The respondent’s complaint was directed against a specific act of the Bank in the administration of her deposit account. She alleged that the Bank altered the category of the account without her authority and asked that the alteration be reversed. Deciding that complaint would require examination of the terms on which the account was opened and maintained, the authority under which the Bank purported to convert it, whether the respondent’s consent was required and obtained, and whether the conversion complied with applicable banking rules and regulatory requirements. On the allegations made and the relief sought, the complaint fell within the jurisdiction of the Banking Mohtasib as a complaint of alleged banking malpractice in the administration of a deposit account.

11. Consequently, the appeal is allowed, the judgment dated 13.04.2026 passed by the learned Consumer Court, Abbottabad, is set aside, and the respondent’s complaint is dismissed for want of jurisdiction. The respondent shall be at liberty to approach the Banking Mohtasib for redressal of her grievance, subject to the applicable statutory requirements.
